pl-l4d1c4-d1e112.summary: Distinguishes natural signs, like smoke signifying fire, from given signs; among given signs some are sacraments and some not, since every sacrament is a sign but not conversely.
claims: Every sacrament is a sign, but not every sign is a sacrament.

pl-l4d1c4-d1e118.summary: Holds that a sacrament bears the likeness of what it signifies, since otherwise it would not properly be a sacrament, as Augustine says. A sacrament is properly so a sign of God's grace and form of invisible grace that it bears its image and is its cause. So sacraments were instituted not only to signify but also to sanctify.
claims: A sacrament bears the likeness of what it signifies.
A sacrament properly is both image and cause of grace.
Sacraments were instituted to sanctify, not only to signify.

pl-l4d1c4-d1e124.summary: States that what was instituted only to signify is merely a sign, not a sacrament, like the carnal sacrifices and ceremonial observances of the old law, which could never make the offerers just. As Paul says, the blood of goats and the ashes of a heifer sanctified the unclean for cleanness of the flesh, not of the soul, the uncleanness being contact with the dead.
claims: Signs instituted only to signify are not sacraments in the proper sense.
The sacrifices of the old law cleansed the flesh, not the soul.

pl-l4d1c4-d1e127.summary: Quotes Augustine: the uncleanness the Law cleanses is only contact with a dead man, which made one unclean for seven days; one was purified by the Law on the third and seventh day so as to enter the temple.
claims: The Law's purifications removed ritual impurity from contact with the dead.

pl-l4d1c4-d1e137.summary: Adds that the legal rites sometimes cleansed bodily leprosy, but no one was ever justified by works of the Law, as Paul says, even when they were done in faith and charity, because God imposed them as servitude, not justification, and as a figure of the future, wanting them offered to him rather than to idols. They were signs, and also sacraments in a less proper sense, as signs of a sacred thing they did not confer; Paul calls 'works of the Law' those instituted only to signify or as a burden.
claims: No one was justified by works of the Law.
The legal rites were imposed as servitude and figure.
The old rites are called sacraments only less properly.

pl-l4d1c4.summary: Distinguishes natural signs, like smoke signifying fire, from given signs, some of which are sacraments: every sacrament is a sign, but not conversely. A sacrament bears the likeness of what it signifies and, properly, is a sign of God's grace and form of invisible grace in such a way that it bears its image and is its cause; sacraments were instituted to sanctify, not only to signify. Signs instituted only to signify, like the sacrifices and ceremonies of the old law, are mere signs: they cleansed the flesh, from contact with the dead or from leprosy, but never justified, even when done in faith and charity, since God imposed them as servitude and figure. They are called sacraments less properly, as signs of a sacred thing they did not confer.
claims: Signs are natural or given; some given signs are sacraments.
Every sacrament is a sign, but not every sign is a sacrament.
A sacrament properly bears the likeness of grace and causes it.
Sacraments were instituted to sanctify as well as to signify.
The rites of the old law signified but did not justify.
